Chapter 1: The Stories We’re Told and the Ones We Never Hear
Have you ever noticed how history class can feel like a long list of names, dates, and places—all marching along in perfect order?
Most lessons start with ancient Greece or Rome, skip over to the Renaissance, and then suddenly, we’re in the modern world. It’s as if the rest of the globe was just backstage, waiting for its cue.
On the surface, the story seems neat and logical—until someone starts seeing the gaps. Imagine sitting in a classroom, glancing up at a map that’s all about Europe, and realizing your own family’s history isn’t anywhere to be found in the textbook. At first, it’s a quiet discomfort, easy to ignore. But with every lesson that skips over entire continents, that feeling just grows. Now, think about the stories you hear at home. Maybe a grandparent shares memories of a bustling village, full of art, trade, and leadership—long before outsiders showed up. These stories are rich and vivid, but they rarely make their way into what we’re taught at school. The contrast can be pretty striking. On one hand, there’s this polished narrative of progress and civilization; on the other, there’s a living memory of worlds that seem erased or forgotten. And here’s something to pay attention to—the way history is taught isn’t just random. It’s always been shaped by those in power. The stories that make it into the curriculum usually serve a purpose: to justify control, create a sense of superiority, or maybe to gloss over uncomfortable truths. What we’re left with is a version of the past that seems complete, but is really full of holes. For a lot of people, the realization comes slowly. It might be a teacher who brushes aside a question about African kingdoms, or a textbook that calls colonization a “civilizing” mission. The message is hard to miss: some histories are valued, and others aren’t. Over time, this starts to shape how people see themselves and the world. It becomes easy to think that greatness only comes from certain places, or that some cultures have always been on the sidelines. But let’s step back for a second. The truth is so much more complicated. Across Africa, Asia, and the Americas, civilizations rose and fell, exchanged ideas and goods, and shaped the world in ways that still matter today. These aren’t just footnotes—they’re central to understanding how the world really came to be. Yet, their stories are often hidden, distorted, or left out altogether. The impact of this selective storytelling is huge. It doesn’t just affect what we know; it changes how we see ourselves and each other. When you never hear about your ancestors’ achievements, it’s easy to start believing you’re less than. When entire societies are only described in relation to Europe, their own histories get pushed aside. The journey to reclaim these stories isn’t just about correcting the record. It’s about really understanding the forces that shaped our present—and recognizing how powerful stories can be. Every time a story is told, it shapes identity, belonging, and possibility. So the real challenge is to look beyond the official version, to dig for the voices that have been silenced, and to ask—who benefits from the stories we keep hearing? In classrooms, around dinner tables, and throughout communities, the work of uncovering these hidden histories is always in motion. It takes curiosity, persistence, and the courage to question what seems obvious. Most of all, it requires us to remember that history isn’t just about what’s already happened. It’s about the present—and the future we dare to imagine.
